title: Viagra May Slow Cancer Spread by Blocking Tumour Cholesterol, Major Study Finds
excerpt: Israeli researchers report that sildenafil disrupts a key cholesterol pathway cancer cells use to metastasise, with better survival seen in a 40,000-patient analysis.
body:
• A study led by Israel's Weizmann Institute found that sildenafil, Viagra's active ingredient, blocks a cholesterol pathway cancer cells use to metastasise.
  • Analysis of 20 years of anonymised medical records from roughly five million patients showed improved survival among cancer patients who had taken sildenafil before diagnosis.
  • Combining sildenafil with statins further strengthened the anti-metastatic effect in both lab experiments and observational data.
  • Experts caution that the findings are preclinical and require validation through human clinical trials before informing treatment protocols.

Sildenafil, the active ingredient in the erectile dysfunction drug Viagra, may interfere with cancer cells' ability to spread through the body by disrupting their access to cholesterol, according to a study published in the journal Cancer Research. The findings, led by researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, open a potential new front in cancer treatment using an existing, widely prescribed medication.

How the Mechanism Works

The research team uncovered a previously unknown biological pathway through which sildenafil affects cholesterol regulation inside cells. Cancer cells depend on cholesterol to detach from primary tumours and invade other organs — a process known as metastasis, which is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths. By limiting cholesterol access through a mechanism called PDE5a inhibition, sildenafil appears to make it harder for tumours to spread.

"We have uncovered a new biological pathway that links a well-known signaling molecule to cholesterol regulation within cells, and shown how this pathway can be harnessed to interfere with the ability of cancer cells to form metastases."

— Ayelet Erez, Weizmann Institute of Science

The study combined laboratory mouse models and human cancer cell cultures with a large-scale analysis of real-world patient data. Scientists from Clalit Health Services, Israel's largest health organisation, analysed more than 20 years of anonymised medical records from approximately five million participants, including an observational study of 40,000 males diagnosed with cancer.

Real-World Patient Data

The observational analysis showed that male cancer patients who had taken sildenafil before their diagnosis had better overall survival rates than those who had not used the drug. Survival rates improved further among patients who had taken both sildenafil and statins — cholesterol-lowering drugs already widely prescribed for heart disease.

"This study bridges two worlds," said Samah Hayek, a senior epidemiologist at the Clalit Research Institute and study co-author. "The laboratory identified a promising biological mechanism while Clalit's real-world data showed that the same signal may also be reflected in patient outcomes."

The researchers stressed that the improved survival was observed only in males who had used Viagra before their cancer diagnosis, and the study did not evaluate whether starting the drug after diagnosis would produce similar benefits. The research also did not assess whether the same effects would apply to women, since sildenafil is predominantly prescribed to men.

Expert Reactions and Caveats

Independent experts expressed cautious optimism. S. Adam Ramin, a urologic oncologist at Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, called the study "well-designed" and said it "appears to have real applications in real-world situations."

Mike Lattanzi, director of the Genitourinary Cancer Research Program at Texas Oncology, offered a more measured assessment. "These results are preclinical — meaning the data were derived from cell lines or mice," he said. "They would need to be validated in human studies in order to inform the management of cancer patients."

"One of the reasons this is such an interesting study is that the molecules they used to treat the cancer cells are medications many people already take on a daily basis."

— Mike Lattanzi, Texas Oncology

Ramkishen Narayanan, a urologic oncologist at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in California, described the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway mechanism as "exciting" but cautioned that "the ability to reliably translate the findings to real-world clinical scenarios is still very limited."

What Comes Next

The study was a collaboration between the Weizmann Institute, Clalit Health Services, and the U.S. National Cancer Institute. Researchers say the next step would be clinical trials to test whether sildenafil — either alone or in combination with statins — can be incorporated into existing cancer treatment protocols. With more than two million new cancer cases diagnosed annually in the United States alone, a repurposed drug that is already considered safe could offer a significant advantage if clinical trials confirm the preclinical promise.
